one_liner: AVX2 bitmap rewrite of picohttpparser's header scanner; 1.7-1.8x the SSE4.2 PCMPESTRI version on Haswell.
what_it_does: A one-commit fork of picohttpparser (the HTTP/1 parser used by H2O and Perl's Plack/Starman) that swaps in an AVX2 version of parse_headers when the file is compiled with -mavx2. The API does not change: phr_parse_request, phr_parse_response, phr_parse_headers and phr_decode_chunked take a caller-owned buffer and fill pointer/length pairs. They allocate nothing and keep no state. Without __AVX2__ the file compiles to stock December 2014 picohttpparser.
how_it_is_fast: Upstream finds each delimiter with SSE4.2 PCMPESTRI. That instruction covers 16 bytes, has about 11 cycles of latency and runs once per token, so short header fields make the parser latency-bound (the blog puts the ceiling at about 1.45 bytes/cycle). The fork classifies 128 bytes at a time with plain AVX2 compare/and/or ops, treating bytes as signed so that 0x00-0x1F, ':', TAB and DEL can be tested without unsigned compares. It packs the results with PMOVMSKB into two 128-bit bitmaps, one for name/value delimiters and one for line ends, then walks them with TZCNT and reuses them across several headers before rescanning, which trades one latency-bound search per token for bulk, throughput-bound classification.
when_to_use: Studying or porting the technique: the whole change is a single ~309-line diff to picohttpparser.c, a compact example of replacing per-token PCMPESTRI searches with 128-byte AVX2 bitmaps plus TZCNT.

Throughput experiments on x86-64 Haswell-or-newer CPUs where HTTP/1 header scanning dominates CPU time and requests run a few hundred bytes with many headers (the benchmark requests were 430 and 703 bytes, 9 headers each).

Parsing complete, well-formed header blocks from a trusted source (behind a proxy that already validated framing, or replaying captured traffic), where you can guarantee the whole header block is in the buffer before calling.
A/B testing against picohttpparser without touching call sites, because the four exported functions keep the 2014 upstream signatures.
when_not_to_use: Internet-facing servers parsing untrusted or partially received requests. Reading the code, malformed header names and values are accepted, and truncated input can move the cursor past len (see gotchas). The author's own PR says the code 'was not tested much, so it might contain some bugs'.
Peers that send bare-LF line endings: the AVX2 path returns -1 for them, while upstream and the fork's non-AVX2 path accept them.

Portable binaries: AVX2 is chosen at compile time with no runtime dispatch, so a -mavx2 build needs a Haswell-class CPU. Windows (LLP64), MSVC and C++ builds are also out because the code uses GNU inline asm, void* arithmetic and 64-bit unsigned long shifts.

Chunked bodies from untrusted peers: phr_decode_chunked is the 2014 code. It lacks upstream's 2023-2025 hardening (rejecting suspicious chunk sizes, capping chunk overhead, requiring CRLF in chunk headers) and has no phr_decode_chunked_is_in_data.
Anything that needs upstream's later fixes or testing: upstream is 98 commits ahead of the fork's base, including ASan/UBSan CI and MSVC/g++ build fixes.

integration.min_toolchain: C with GNU extensions (void* arithmetic, AT&T inline asm) on GCC or Clang with -mavx2 (the published build used GCC 4.9.2 -O3 -mavx2 -mbmi2); not MSVC, not compilable as C++
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 and TZCNT (Haswell or newer) on an LP64 OS (Linux/macOS/BSD) for the fast path; other targets get the 2014 SSE4.2/scalar code
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The functions are stateless, allocate nothing and only read static const tables, so concurrent calls on separate buffers are safe by construction.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same four functions and signatures as 2014 picohttpparser, so it is a one-file swap, but it behaves differently on malformed or truncated input and lacks upstream's later API (phr_decode_chunked_is_in_data) and hardening

gotchas: The AVX2 code is only on the 'avx2' branch; 'master' is unmodified upstream from 2014-12-16. The Makefile and .travis.yml never pass -mavx2, so 'make test' only exercises the old code path.

The header-name scan stops at any byte 0x00-0x1F as well as ':' and never checks that it stopped on ':'. As a result 'a\0b: c' parses as name 'a' with value 'b: c' instead of returning -1, and by my reading the fork's own 'NUL/CTL in header name' tests would fail under -mavx2.

'two_char & 0x0a == 0x0a' parses as 'two_char & 1' because == binds tighter than &. So bare-LF line endings are rejected, while a lone CR, ESC or DEL ends a header value instead of producing an error ('CTL in header value' test).

Despite the 128-byte window, callers need no buffer alignment (all loads are unaligned). For the final <128 bytes, though, the bitmap comes from an uninitialized 32-byte stack copy, zero padding or a stale upper half, and '*(unsigned short*)buf' reads 2 bytes. So by code reading, a truncated first parse (last_len=0) can advance past len instead of returning -2.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose it only when you specifically want picohttpparser's C API with this AVX2 bitmap design, for study or a controlled experiment. The siblings saw commits in 2025-2026: httpp (header-only C, which reports ~2.26x over picohttpparser on its own hardware), hparse (Zig SIMD, streaming) and picohttpparser-rs (a safe-Rust port that reports 133,352 differential cases matching the C original), so they are the better production picks.
verified_claims_summary: On a Haswell i5-4278U with turbo off, built with GCC 4.9.2 -O3 -mavx2 -mbmi2, the AVX2 build parsed bench.c's 703-byte, 9-header request 1.79x faster than December 2014 picohttpparser's PCMPESTRI path (6.96M vs 3.90M per second, consistent with 10M iterations taking 1.436 s vs 2.564 s), and fukamachi.c's 430-byte request 1.68x faster (8.06M vs 4.81M). The fukamachi figures match a 100,000-iteration loop, so those runs lasted only about 12-21 ms; both tests repeatedly parse one complete, hot-cache request.
status_note: Abandoned since its single 2014-12-18 commit and never merged upstream (h2o/picohttpparser PR #10 closed in 2020). It is MIT/Perl dual-licensed and a single .c/.h pair, so it is easy to vendor, but treat it as a prototype that needs an audit and fuzzing before use.
